newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay stocks in 3-day rally, falter near 4,000.
newsitem.headline: Bombay stocks in 3-day rally, falter near 4,000.

text.p: Bombay shares ended with smart gains on Thursday spurred by heavy fund buying in front-bencher stocks, but the market faces a tough task to cross the psychological 4,000 barrrier, traders said.
"The trend continues to be bullish," said R. Ramakrishnan, chief dealer at ASK-Raymond James Securities India. "The market seems to be shifting to a new range of 3,800-4,100 level."
Market action was focused on front-line shares, with some second-tier stocks attracting profit-booking by investors and local institutions, players said.

Bombay's 30-share index-- the market barometer ended 53 points, or 1.35 percent higher, at 3,980.58 taking the market into a three-day rally -- racing 145 points, or nearly four percent in its winning streak.
Funds were keen buyers in multinationals -- Hindustan Lever, Nestle, oil refineries -- Hindustan Petroleum, Bharat Petroleum and Gas Authority of India and software stocks, traders said.
A consolidation in share prices at current levels could pave the way for an extended rally, players said.
"Looking at the market mood, the index should cross the 4,000-level in this phase itself," said Govind Agarwal, institutional sales dealer at Motilal Oswal Securities.
"If it crosses 4,000 and remains there for a day or two, then we could see it going up to the 4,200 level."
Bombay's rally has been mostly driven by aggressive foreign fund buying based on hopes of a reversal in a slowing economy, traders said.

Last week the government reported that industrial output -- a key barometer for the overall economy -- inched up by only 2.4 percent in February over the same month in 1996. The growth rate in February 1996 was a blistering 13.3 percent.
Tight credit, slack demand, heavy inventories and lack of power contributed to the growth slowdown.

But analysts said they expect output to gather momentum in the third and fourth quarters of 1997/98 -- six months from September 1997 -- as the effects of increased bank credit, falling interest rates, lower corporate taxes and agricultural growth take hold.
"Indications are that the worst is over and the economy is reviving," said Sanjay Vaid, chief trader at local firm, Lloyds Securites.
The market outlook remained bullish, but the rally could be arrested by end-account factors on Friday, traders said.
"It's the last day of weekly trade, so we can expect a minor correction," said Antony Sequeira, managing director at Arcadia Share & Stock Brokers.
